Fusing Climate Data Products Using a Spatially Varying Autoencoder

    
    Fusing Climate Data Products Using a Spatially Varying Autoencoder

    
    Jacob A. Johnson, Matthew J. Heaton, William F. Christensen, Lynsie R. Warr, and Summer B. Rupper

    
    
      Journal of Agricultural, Biological and Environmental Statistics 31(2), 273–286
      June 2026
    

    
    
     Winner, 2024 ASA Section on Statistics and the Environment Student Paper Competition
    

    
    
    
     Paper  Preprint  Code  Slides  Poster 
    

    
    
    
      Abstract
      Autoencoders are powerful machine learning models used to compress information from multiple data sources. However, autoencoders, like all artificial neural networks, are often unidentifiable and uninterpretable. This research focuses on creating an identifiable and interpretable autoencoder that can be used to meld and combine climate data products. The proposed autoencoder utilizes a Bayesian statistical framework, allowing for probabilistic interpretations while also varying spatially to capture useful spatial patterns across the various data products. Constraints are placed on the autoencoder as it learns patterns in the data, creating an interpretable consensus that includes the important features from each input. We demonstrate the utility of the autoencoder by combining information from multiple precipitation products in High Mountain Asia.
    
    

    

  
  
  
  

    
    Minibatch Markov Chain Monte Carlo Algorithms for Fitting Gaussian Processes

    
    Minibatch Markov Chain Monte Carlo Algorithms for Fitting Gaussian Processes

    
    Matthew J. Heaton and Jacob A. Johnson

    
    
      Bayesian Analysis 21(1), 21–43
      March 2026
    

    
    

    
    
    
     Paper  Preprint  Code  Slides  Poster 
    

    
    
    
      Abstract
      Gaussian processes (GPs) are a highly flexible, nonparametric statistical model that are commonly used to fit nonlinear relationships or account for correlation between observations. However, the computational load of fitting a Gaussian process is \(\mathcal{O}(n^3)\) making them infeasible for use on large datasets. To make GPs more feasible for large datasets, this research focuses on the use of minibatching to estimate GP parameters. Specifically, we outline both approximate and exact minibatch Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms that substantially reduce the computation of fitting a GP by only considering small subsets of the data at a time. We demonstrate and compare this methodology using various simulations and real datasets.

I’m a third-year PhD student at the University of Wisconsin–Madison working with Dr. Matthias Katzfuß. My research is focused on finding new methods in spatial statistics, Gaussian processes, and uncertainty quantification, specifically with applications in climate and environmental science. Currently, I am working on state-space models involving non-Gaussian forecasts.
Before starting my PhD, I got a Bachelor’s degree from Brigham Young University where I did research with Dr. Matthew Heaton. I recently completed a year-round statistics internship at Sandia National Laboratories where I worked with Dr. Katherine Goode. I’m originally from Lindon, Utah, and my hobbies include watching college sports, camping, hiking, and spending time with my family.
You can find my publications, talks, and CV on this site. The best way to reach me is by email at jajohnsonstats at gmail dot com.

  Functional Labeling of Wisconsin Environments

  
  Functional Labeling of Wisconsin Environments

  
  
  
    FWE 711 Course project
    May 2025
  
  

  
  
  A latent-variable framework that uses satellite imagery to group Wisconsin landscapes by how they responded to the 2021 summer drought.
  

  
  
  
   Report  Slides 
  

  
  
  
    Abstract
    Understanding why ecosystems exhibit varying resilience to climate stress is a critical challenge in modern ecology. This study proposes a multi-step latent variable framework to examine modes of ecological vulnerability during the summer 2021 drought in Wisconsin. Utilizing high-resolution satellite imagery data, the proposed model decoupled 10-year historical environmental baselines from acute stress responses. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) condensed static landscape and climate variables, while Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) distilled collinear satellite metrics into two latent axes of stress response. Applying K-means clustering to these reduced dimensions naturally partitioned the state into three geographical vulnerability archetypes.
